text: Design the review before it starts
After this you can set an audit scope, evidence plan and completion criteria.

An audit plan sets the question to be answered and defines how evidence will be collected. It names the item, version, objective, participants, sample, documents, schedule and the authority that receives findings. Good planning separates what will be tested from what will be inspected. It also specifies what counts as a finding and how corrections are verified. An audit with an undefined boundary can finish on time but still miss the important mismatch.

items: Name the product, revision and audit purpose. You should see: Everyone shares the same target. If not: Resolve unconfirmed item identity.
Map requirements and parts to evidence. You should see: Each material question has a planned check. If not: Ask for missing records before the review.
Assign roles, schedule and sampling method. You should see: Participants know what they must bring. If not: Record limitations of any sample.
Set finding, escalation and closure rules. You should see: Decisions will not be improvised at the end. If not: Confirm the approving role before beginning.
Inferred: An audit samples units from two batches. Reviewers check tests, labels and installed software versions.

text: Plan around a clear audit question, not just a meeting date.
A sample cannot automatically prove every unsampled item is identical.

items: Starting without an agreed configuration Reviewers may evaluate different versions. Fix: Freeze and record the audit target first.
